- typesafe:typesafe-ai: Build AI-powered software with TypeSafe: small units of AI intelligence you can use like programming primitives. Its System One models, including Jev, turn natural language and application state into typed judgments and probabilities that code can combine. Use when a feature needs programmable common sense, when brainstorming what AI could make possible in an app, or when an LLM prompt-and-parse step could become a structured decision. Applications include routing, ranking, extraction, verification, and interactive experiences; these are starting points, not the limits. Read live docs and cookbooks to find useful patterns and discover new combinations.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- plugin-authoring: Make a mod: a change to Claude's own interface or behaviour, such as a live pane or panel, a band above the prompt, a status line, a toast, a slash command, or a hook on tool calls or prompts. Use to make, change or debug a mod or its hooks module.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- anthropic-skills:built-in-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses the built-in browser, the browser pane inside the Claude desktop app (also called the in-app browser, the browser pane, Claude's browser, or "your own browser"), whose tools are named mcp__Claude_Browser__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser tool instead. It covers the pane's persistent sign-ins, tabs and preview_start, reading pages as text, site approvals, what the pane cannot open, and what to do when it cannot be reached. It is not for Claude in Chrome (mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:chrome-browser: Read this skill before the first step that uses Claude in Chrome, the browser extension whose tools are named mcp__claude-in-chrome__* (also called Chrome, the browser extension, or the external browser) and which acts in the person's real Chrome with their own sign-ins; before those tools are turned on there may be a single enable__mcp__claude-in-chrome tool instead. It covers loading the tools in one ToolSearch call, checking the person's open tabs and working in a new tab, site permissions, GIF recordings, console logs, dialogs to avoid, and when to stop and ask. It is not for the built-in browser (mcp__Claude_Browser__* or mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__* tools), which has its own skill, and it does not decide which browser to use.
- anthropic-skills:computer-use: Read this skill before the first step of any request to do something in an app on the person's own computer (Notes, Finder, System Settings, any desktop app), to look at their screen, or for "computer use". Computer use (desktop control) lets Claude take screenshots of the person's desktop and control it with clicks, typing and scrolling through the Claude desktop app; its tools are named mcp__computer-use__* when the session runs in the desktop app and mcp__remote-devices__computer_* when a cloud session is linked to the person's computer; before computer use is turned on for a conversation there may be no such tools, only an enable__mcp__remote-devices__computer tool, which turns it on. It covers turning it on, picking the right tool, the access flow, and the safety rules for tiered apps, links and financial actions. It is not for websites, which go through Claude in Chrome or the built-in browser and their own skills.
- anthropic-skills:deep-research: Use this skill when the user's prompt requires (1) researching a topic across multiple sources, comparing options or alternatives, analyzing trends or history, understanding markets or industries, or reviewing literature or studies and (2) synthesizing that research into a comprehensive, narrative report. If you're planning to search the web or internal knowledge bases, consider using this skill. This skill coordinates research subagents, so use it only when you have a tool for spawning subagents (the Agent or Task tool); otherwise, research the question directly.
- anthropic-skills:docs: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:google-workspace: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:setup-writing-style: Learns how the user writes from their own sent messages and docs, and builds a voice profile so future drafts sound like them instead of generic AI. The profile is saved as the my-writing-style skill. Use when the user asks to set up, learn, or capture their writing voice, or complains that drafts sound generic or unlike them and no my-writing-style profile exists. Only for drafting text the user will send as themselves, not for Claude's own replies.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
</system-reminder>

<system-reminder>
While auto mode is active:

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools. The choice is yours: prefer Edit or Write when a shell edit would be fragile, such as exact or multi-line replacements, or sed/awk flags that differ between GNU and BSD/macOS.

content.content:
## Redrawing

The window stays fast while something animates or updates. It is split into views that are each drawn again only when their own state changes, never rebuilt whole from the main window down on every frame. The views are the body's tab bar, where the Chat tab and task tabs show their spinners; the message list; each task's output; the Tasks tab; the chat input; each sidebar; and the Planning board. A spinner turning, a running task's time counting up every second, as the [MessageListStatus](../prompt-mode/message-list/Status.md#message-list-status) says, or a reply streaming in redraws only the view that shows it, never the rest of the body, the tab bar, the sidebars, the Tasks tab, the chat input, or an open Planning board.
This holds for the window as a whole what each part already holds on its own: a table's rows, as [TableDrawing](../../ui/components/table/Drawing.md#table-drawing) says, a task's streamed output, as [TaskTableScrolling](../../ui/components/task-table/Scrolling.md#task-table-scrolling) says, the message list, as [MessageListScrolling](../prompt-mode/message-list/Scrolling.md#message-list-scrolling) says, and the Tasks tab's running rows, as [TasksTab.virtualized](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#virtualized) says. Within a view drawn again, those rules still decide what is laid out anew.
A slide still moves every part of the body together, frame by frame, as [Body.sliding](./Body.md#sliding) says. A view whose width changes is laid out anew at each width as the slide goes, so being drawn only on a change of its own never leaves one at its old width until the slide settles.
A test shows it: while a task runs and nothing else changes, the Tasks tab, the chat input, and the sidebars are not drawn again from one frame to the next; and while a right sidebar slides out, the tab bar, the message list, and the chat input are laid out at each width as it goes.

## Debug Log

[DebugLog](../debug-log/index.md#debug-log)

## Sandbox

[Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox)

## File Ownership

Every file and folder the application creates belongs to the user running it, as one the user made in Explorer or a terminal would, on every platform, so the user never has to take ownership of anything, or change its permissions, to edit, move, or delete it, or for git, piton, or the harness to use it. That goes for a new project's folder and everything written into it, the project's data under .suspense, the files a task or the editor writes, and the application's own files, as its preferences.
On Windows, the application never asks to run as administrator: its build declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it, as invoked, and never requires elevation, nor does its installer start it elevated once it is installed, nor its self-update when it starts the new version. Should it be run elevated all the same, as from an administrator's terminal, what it creates is still the user's: each file and folder is made owned by the user who is signed in, never by the Administrators group, and takes the permissions it inherits from the folder it is in, never permissions of its own. The same holds for what the programs it starts create, git's repository included, so git never refuses a project for being owned by someone else. Nothing the application creates is ever left owned by Administrators, SYSTEM, or another account.

## Name

The application is called Suspense.

## Project Files

[ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data)

## Theme

[Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme)

## Main Window

[MainWindow](./MainWindow.md#main-window)

## User Preferences

[UserPreferences](../user-preferences/index.md#user-preferences)

## Edge Releases

[EdgeReleases](../edge-releases/index.md#edge-releases)

## Self Update

[SelfUpdate](../self-update/index.md#self-update)

## Redrawing

The window stays fast while something animates or updates. It is split into views that are each drawn again only when their own state changes, never rebuilt whole from the main window down on every frame. The views are the body's tab bar, where the Chat tab and task tabs show their spinners; the message list; each task's output; the Tasks tab; the chat input; each sidebar; and the Planning board. A spinner turning, a running task's time counting up every second, as the [MessageListStatus](../prompt-mode/message-list/Status.md#message-list-status) says, or a reply streaming in redraws only the view that shows it, never the rest of the body, the tab bar, the sidebars, the Tasks tab, the chat input, or an open Planning board.
This holds for the window as a whole what each part already holds on its own: a table's rows, as [TableDrawing](../../ui/components/table/Drawing.md#table-drawing) says, a task's streamed output, as [TaskTableScrolling](../../ui/components/task-table/Scrolling.md#task-table-scrolling) says, the message list, as [MessageListScrolling](../prompt-mode/message-list/Scrolling.md#message-list-scrolling) says, and the Tasks tab's running rows, as [TasksTab.virtualized](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/tasks/index.md#virtualized) says. Within a view drawn again, those rules still decide what is laid out anew.
A slide still moves every part of the body together, frame by frame, as [Body.sliding](./Body.md#sliding) says. A view whose width changes is laid out anew at each width as the slide goes, so being drawn only on a change of its own never leaves one at its old width until the slide settles.
A test shows it: while a task runs and nothing else changes, the Tasks tab, the chat input, and the sidebars are not drawn again from one frame to the next; and while a right sidebar slides out, the tab bar, the message list, and the chat input are laid out at each width as it goes.

## Debug Log

[DebugLog](../debug-log/index.md#debug-log)

## Sandbox

[Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox)

## File Ownership

Every file and folder the application creates belongs to the user running it, as one the user made in Explorer or a terminal would, on every platform, so the user never has to take ownership of anything, or change its permissions, to edit, move, or delete it, or for git, piton, or the harness to use it. That goes for a new project's folder and everything written into it, the project's data under .suspense, the files a task or the editor writes, and the application's own files, as its preferences.
On Windows, the application never asks to run as administrator: its build declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it, as invoked, and never requires elevation, nor does its installer start it elevated once it is installed, nor its self-update when it starts the new version. Should it be run elevated all the same, as from an administrator's terminal, what it creates is still the user's: each file and folder is made owned by the user who is signed in, never by the Administrators group, and takes the permissions it inherits from the folder it is in, never permissions of its own. The same holds for what the programs it starts create, git's repository included, so git never refuses a project for being owned by someone else. Nothing the application creates is ever left owned by Administrators, SYSTEM, or another account.

## Name

The application is called Suspense.

content.content:
## Virtualized

The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.
Scrolled to its bottom, the last row shows whole, its bottom edge at the bottom of the tab's visible area, never cut off by even a pixel, and nothing lies beneath it but the list's own bottom padding of 8 pixels. The list's height is the sum of its rows, headings and day dividers included, and that padding, measured in the same device pixels the rows are drawn at, and its scrollable height is that less the height of the area it is drawn in: the right sidebar's own visible area, never an area that counts a sticky heading, the open task's back bar, or the scrollbar's own room as part of the list. Headings pinned at the bottom take room from the list's visible area, as those at the top do, so scrolled to the bottom, the last row still shows whole above any heading pinned there, and none ever hides a row. However the tab is resized, by the window, the sidebar's panels, or the sidebar's width, the bottom is worked out anew in that frame, so a list scrolled to its bottom still shows its last row whole.

# Message List Status

## Sliding

Whenever something slides out or back along one of the body's edges, as the [RightSidebar](../../ui/components/right-sidebar/index.md#right-sidebar) does, everything else in the body moves smoothly with it, frame by frame, rather than jumping once the slide is over: the tab bar, the selected tab's contents, the Ask conversation while it shows, and the chat input all keep their right edge against the sliding edge throughout, so they narrow or widen together, in step with it and with each other. None of them lags behind another, is left at its old width until the slide settles, or runs beneath what is sliding. Their contents are laid out anew at each width as it changes, text wrapping and rows reflowing as they go: the tab bar's tabs, the chat input's text and buttons, the message list's table, and an open file's editor. A slide that reverses partway moves them back from wherever it had reached.

content.content:
## Virtualized

The list is virtualized: however many tasks the project has run, it lays out and draws only the rows in view, and a few rows either side of it, never every row, so opening the tab, scrolling it, resizing the sidebar, filtering, and new tasks arriving cost the same with ten thousand previous tasks as with ten. Every row is 28 pixels tall, section headings included, so where each row lies is known from its place in the list alone, without laying out the rows before it, and the scrollbar's thumb is sized and placed from the whole list's height, as though every row were drawn.
A row is drawn only from what its row shows, its mode, status, first line, and time, read from each task's history record once and kept, never by reading a record's output, lines, or snapshots while scrolling; those are read only when a task is opened. Running rows update their time and spinner in place, redrawing only what is in view. Scrolling to a row, as when the tab opens on Running, a filter changes, or a queued row is dragged past the edge, jumps straight to its place without drawing the rows between. A row scrolled out of view and back is the same as it was, its selection and highlight kept. A pinned heading sits over the list without moving any row, so where each row lies is unchanged by it.
Scrolling past either end does nothing: with the list at its top or its bottom, a wheel, trackpad, or drag that goes further leaves every row exactly where it is, frame after frame, with no stretch, bounce, or nudge of even a pixel and back, and draws nothing anew, since nothing moved. Its scroll position is clamped to its ends before a frame is drawn, never drawn past an end and corrected the frame after, and kept in whole device pixels, so a row never shimmers between two places. What lies at an end stays at it: a running row's time ticking, a task finishing, a row added or removed elsewhere in the list, or the tab being resized never makes the rows in view jump and settle. A list scrolled to its bottom stays at its bottom as rows are added, and one at its top stays at its top. The list counts as taller than the tab only once it overflows it by a whole pixel, as the right sidebar's panels do, so a list that fits never scrolls at all.
Scrolled to its bottom, the last row shows whole, its bottom edge at the bottom of the tab's visible area, never cut off by even a pixel, and nothing lies beneath it but the list's own bottom padding of 8 pixels. The list's height is the sum of its rows, headings and day dividers included, and that padding, measured in the same device pixels the rows are drawn at, and its scrollable height is that less the height of the area it is drawn in: the right sidebar's own visible area, never an area that counts a sticky heading, the open task's back bar, or the scrollbar's own room as part of the list. Headings pinned at the bottom take room from the list's visible area, as those at the top do, so scrolled to the bottom, the last row still shows whole above any heading pinned there, and none ever hides a row. However the tab is resized, by the window, the sidebar's panels, or the sidebar's width, the bottom is worked out anew in that frame, so a list scrolled to its bottom still shows its last row whole.

## Days

Within Previous, tasks are grouped by the day they were sent, in the user's local time, each day headed by a divider row, 28 pixels tall like every row, its label in small muted text set in to line up with the rows' text: "Today", "Yesterday", the weekday for the rest of the past week, as "Tuesday", and the date beyond that, as "3 October", with the year added once it isn't this one, as "28 September 2025", then, muted after it, how many tasks that day holds. Days run oldest to newest, as the tasks do, and only days with a task are shown; a chain is under the day its first step was sent. While filters are on, a day with no task shown is left out, and its count is of the tasks shown. The labels follow the clock: one reading "Today" reads "Yesterday" once midnight has passed, without reopening the tab.
A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks had; a session that starts a new conversation shows a small muted mark at its first row's right instead, its tooltip saying it started a new conversation.

Headings pinned at the bottom take room from the list's visible area, as those at the top do, so scrolled to the bottom, the last row still shows whole above any heading pinned there, and none ever hides a row. However the tab is resized, by the window, the sidebar's panels, or the sidebar's width, the bottom is worked out anew in that frame, so a list scrolled to its bottom still shows its last row whole.

## Days

Within Previous, tasks are grouped by the day they were sent, in the user's local time, each day headed by a divider row, 28 pixels tall like every row, its label in small muted text set in to line up with the rows' text: "Today", "Yesterday", the weekday for the rest of the past week, as "Tuesday", and the date beyond that, as "3 October", with the year added once it isn't this one, as "28 September 2025", then, muted after it, how many tasks that day holds. Days run oldest to newest, as the tasks do, and only days with a task are shown; a chain is under the day its first step was sent. While filters are on, a day with no task shown is left out, and its count is of the tasks shown. The labels follow the clock: one reading "Today" reads "Yesterday" once midnight has passed, without reopening the tab.
A day's divider is sticky beneath Previous's own heading: while its tasks are scrolled through, it stays pinned just below that heading, until the next day's divider pushes it out, so the day of the rows in view always shows. Day dividers take the place of the session dividers the previous tasks had; a session that starts a new conversation shows a small muted mark at its first row's right instead, its tooltip saying it started a new conversation.

Only the board's cards move this way; steps in an open story, and every other list, are dragged as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, with its line.
A card picked up by its grip lifts off the board as a full-size copy of itself, the same width and height, drawn as the parts draw a story card, tilted a few degrees, about 3, on the theme's overlay surface with its edge border and the soft shadow the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme)'s elevation gives floating surfaces, the one shadow on the board. It follows the pointer, held where it was grabbed, and never takes the mouse. The card's own place in its column becomes the gap it left, empty, the card's height, so the column doesn't jump as it lifts.
Where the card would land, the cards slide apart to open a placeholder the dragged card's height, 8 pixels from the cards either side, as the cards are spaced: a box the card's size on the theme's well surface, with its corners rounded 6 pixels as a card's are, and no border, so it reads as an empty slot. The gap is chosen as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) chooses it, among the cards of the column the pointer is over, and only one is open at a time: as the pointer moves into another gap, or another column, the gap it left closes as the new one opens, and the gap the card came from closes once the pointer leaves its column, opening again if it comes back. A column that takes no drops opens no gap, and its cards never move while a card is dragged over it.
Nothing waits on motion while the user is waiting on it. The gap the card would drop into is updated at once, the moment the pointer crosses the middle of a card, exactly as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, and a drop always goes where the gap was chosen, even while the cards are still sliding toward it; only the sliding of the cards around it is animated, quickly, as below.
Dropped over an open gap, the copy settles into it: it straightens, its shadow fades, and it moves from where it was released into the placeholder, which it then is, the story saved in its new place at the moment of the drop, as every change to the plan is. Dropped anywhere else, or where it began, it settles back into the gap it came from the same way, and nothing changes. Escape while dragging cancels it, settling the card back where it was.
A card moved any other way animates to its new place, as Linear's do, in a quick motion of about 150 milliseconds, eased out, sliding from where it was to where it now is, the cards it passes or leaves sliding to close and open the room it takes, never fading or bouncing. That covers every move the sprint describes: "Move to next sprint", "Move to backlog", and "Move to draft" from a card's menu, or the bulk bar, Alt+Up, Alt+Down, Alt+Left, and Alt+Right, Ctrl+Enter, Send sprint moving its stories into Current sprint, and Close sprint moving them into Done and back to the start of Next sprint. A card added, as by a composer or Duplicate, slides the cards below it down to make room, and a card deleted slides them up to close it, in the same motion. The board scrolls sideways, and a column up or down, to keep a moved card that has focus in view, as the keyboard says. Focus goes with the card at once, not when its motion ends, and the plan is saved at once.
The side panel slides in from the board's right as it opens, in the same quick motion, the board narrowing alongside it, and slides back out to the right as it closes, the board widening as it goes; replacing what it holds with another story, drafting, or research changes its content in place, with no slide. Its content, and focus in it, are there as soon as it starts to open.
The open story's card is kept in view, however the board changes around it. As the side panel opens and the board narrows, the board scrolls sideways alongside it, in the same quick motion, just enough to keep the open story's card fully in view, when it was fully in view before; a card already partly out of view is left where it is. A story opened from anywhere outside the board, as a proposal's "Added to Backlog" or "Added to <story>" link, or a palette or ribbon action that opens one, scrolls the board sideways and its column up or down, in the same motion, just enough that its card is fully in view, then highlights it as the open story. Clicking a card only partly in view opens it and scrolls the board and its column just enough to show it all; a card already fully in view never scrolls anything. Each scroll moves only as far as it must, the card landing at the nearest edge of the view, never centred.
Nothing above the view moves what is in it. In a column scrolled away from its top, a card above the view that is added, deleted, or changes height, as a story's status or step lines arriving in Current sprint, or a sprint closing and its stories leaving, never moves the cards in view: the column's scroll shifts by the same amount, at once and with no motion, so they stay exactly where they were, and the column's thumb moves without jumping, as the [Scrollbar.steadiness](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#steadiness) says. A column at its top keeps its top, and cards in view move as the motion above says.
Every motion here takes about 150 milliseconds, never longer, and a move made while another is still under way starts from wherever the card is then, never queued behind it.

## Layout

Everything in Planning is laid out on one rhythm, so the board scans at a glance. The board fills the body beneath the tab bar, with 24 pixels of padding at its top, sides, and foot. Its columns are all the same fixed width, 320 pixels, 16 pixels apart, each as tall as the board, set side by side from its left edge in the order work moves, Draft, the first, Backlog, Next sprint, Current sprint, Done, and Findings, the last. Each column is a list, as Trello draws one: a container of its own, as the parts draw a list, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base the board is on, its corners rounded 8 pixels, with its heading and its cards inside it, and no border. Three things set a list apart from the board's base, all quieter than any card's state: its recessed surface; the theme's pressed bevel around it, inside its rounded corners, so it reads as sunk into the base; and the 16 pixel gaps between columns. Each column also has a look of its own, telling it from its neighbours: a 2 pixel edge along the list's top, inside its rounded corners and above its heading, in the colour its status icon uses, as the parts give it, laid over the recessed surface at 50%, so Draft's is tertiary text, as the Backlog's is, the two told apart by their icons, Next sprint's secondary text, Current sprint's the accent, Done's success, and Findings' secondary text. The edge is the only place a column's colour shows besides its icon: its heading, its name, its cards, its empty state, and the drag placeholder keep their own surfaces and colours untouched, the placeholder its well surface. Laid over at half strength and 2 pixels tall, a column's edge is always quieter than a card's hover, its selected surface, its focus ring, or the open story's 3 pixel accent line, as the Theme's hierarchy orders decoration below state.
Each column's heading reads as Linear heads a group: a row 32 pixels tall at the list's top, holding, from its left, the column's status icon, 14 pixels, as the parts give it; its name in small semibold text, in the theme's primary text colour; its count beside it, muted; and its actions at its right, each a labelled button, never an icon alone, as the sections give them: "Draft stories" and "Research" on the Backlog; "Send sprint" and "Start automatically" on Next sprint; "Close sprint" on Current sprint, once its sprint can close. A heading with more actions than fit its width wraps them onto a second line beneath its name rather than cutting any off; Draft's heading has no actions but its "+ Add". On Draft, the Backlog, and Next sprint, hovering the heading, or focus anywhere in it, shows "+ Add" just after its count, a small ghost button with a plus icon and its label, never the icon alone, its tooltip saying it adds a story at the top of the list; it takes its room in the heading whether shown or not, so the heading's actions never shift as it appears, and the other columns' headings have none. 8 pixels beneath the heading come its cards, one beneath another, 8 pixels apart, each the list's full inner width.
At the foot of Draft, of the Backlog, and of Next sprint, 8 pixels beneath its last card, or beneath its empty state, is its "Add story" line: a row 32 pixels tall, the list's full inner width, with a plus icon and the label "Add story" in small muted text, its corners rounded 6 pixels, and no border; hovered, it takes the theme's hover surface and its text the theme's primary text colour. It scrolls with the cards, after the last of them. Its composer, as creating says, is drawn where it was clicked, at the foot in the line's place, or at the top, above the first card, from "+ Add": a story card, as the parts draw one, its title a text box in the card's title text, with the focus ring around the card, and beneath it, muted, "Enter to add, Escape to cancel"; the cards below it move down to make room, and the list scrolls to keep it in view. Current sprint, Done, and Findings have no "Add story" line.
Each column scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top while its cards scroll beneath it, inside the list's rounded corners, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) shown along the list's right, inside it, while it holds more than fits. The board scrolls sideways when its columns are wider than the tab, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its foot, laid sideways as [Scrollbar.sideways](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#sideways) says; while they fit, it doesn't scroll. The wheel and the trackpad scroll what is under the pointer, each part of the board on its own. A vertical wheel turn or two-finger swipe over a column, its heading included, scrolls only that column up or down; it never scrolls the board sideways, and it never passes on to the board, not when the column is at its top or its end, nor when it has nothing to scroll. Shift with the wheel, a sideways trackpad swipe, or a mouse's horizontal wheel, tilted or a thumb wheel, anywhere on the board, over a column, its heading, or the padding and gaps around them, scrolls the board sideways while its columns are wider than the tab, and does nothing while they fit. The horizontal wheel never scrolls a column up or down, and it moves the board the way it is turned, right moving the board right and left moving it left. A vertical wheel turn over the board outside every column, on its padding, in the 16 pixel gaps between columns, or in the space beside the last column, scrolls the board sideways instead, as Trello does, down moving it right and up left. A diagonal trackpad swipe over a column scrolls the column up or down and the board sideways together, each by its own share of the swipe, the up and down share to the column and the sideways share to the board. Scrolling over the side panel, the pause bar, or the bulk bar never moves the board or any of its columns: the side panel scrolls only itself, and the two bars scroll nothing. Every card's state reads the same way, as below, and every label is the same small text, muted where it is secondary.
The board is kept as it was left while Planning's tab stays open, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) keeps a tab. Selecting another tab and then Planning's again shows the board scrolled sideways exactly where it was left, and every column scrolled up or down exactly where it was, at once, with nothing animating, sliding, or scrolling into view, as though the tab had never been left; nothing is scrolled to its start or to a card on the way back. A composer is not an opened story but a card being written, and is the one thing drawn in a list, where its story will sit. It is docked at the right of Planning's tab, 400 pixels wide, as tall as the tab, from the tab bar down to the bottom of the body, a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its left edge, and it scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its right while it holds more than fits. Only one thing is in it at a time: opening a story, drafting, or research replaces whatever it held, and closing it leaves nothing there. While it is open the board narrows to the space left of it, its columns keeping their width and scrolling sideways as ever when they no longer fit; the panel never covers the board, and the board never covers it. Closed, it takes no space and the board fills the tab again. It slides in and out at the right, as motion says.
While paused, the pause bar runs across the top of the whole board, above every column, as the paused section says, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it. Each column is headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same five parts, below.

content.text:
Each Planning column now lays out only the cards in view and a few either side. The new test passes, and the rest of the Planning and main-window tests show no new failures.

**The spec doesn't say this yet.** `Planning.layout` in the compiled reference has nothing on how a long column is drawn. I followed your prompt, `Table.drawing` and `Planning.motion` instead. The rule still needs adding to `Planning.layout`.

**What changed in `src/planning.rs`:**
- **Kept heights:** each column remembers how tall every card was laid out. If the column's width changes, every card is measured again.
- **Drawing:** a column draws only its cards in view plus about 320 px either side. The cards out of view take up empty space of the same height, so the scrollbar is sized as though every card were drawn.
- **Measuring the rest:** cards out of view that haven't been measured yet are laid out up to 16 a frame, within 4 ms, until all are known.
- **Always drawn:** the open story's card, the focused card and a card settling from a drop are drawn wherever they are. So opening a story from outside the board jumps straight to its card, and keyboard focus survives scrolling.

**How motion still holds:**
- **Drag gap:** a card that stops being drawn drops its recorded position, so a stale position can't pick the wrong drop gap.
- **Slides:** that card's slide state is also cleared, so it doesn't slide from an old place when it comes back into view.
- **Nothing above moves the view:** the column picks which cards to draw from where the scroll will be once it has adjusted for changes above, so a large change, like a sprint closing, still keeps the cards in view still. For this, `Steady` in `src/animations/steady.rs` now reports which card it is holding still.

**Test:** `a_long_column_draws_only_the_cards_in_view` uses a Backlog of 1,000 stories. It checks that:
- no frame draws more than 40 cards;
- every card gets measured over the following frames;
- once they are, the column's scrollbar holds still;
- opening the last story from outside the board shows its card fully in view without drawing the cards between.

**Test runs:** I ran them in a scratch copy with empty stand-ins for the prompt files the sandbox blocks.
- **Planning:** 5 tests fail. All 5 failed in the earlier full run, before this change.
  - One is `a_dragged_card_finds_its_gap_in_the_column_under_it`, which only tests `choose_gap` with fixed inputs, and I didn't change `choose_gap`.
  - The other 4 are UI tests I didn't look into this time, so I can't say what they need.
- **Main window:** `running_jobs_are_listed_and_revealed` and `new_project_creates_and_opens_a_project` fail; both need `piton`, which the sandbox blocks.

**Limitation:** a card out of view whose content changes keeps its old height until it scrolls into view or the column's width changes. When it comes into view, it's laid out at its real height, and the cards in view stay put.
